'''George Yevick''' (May 8, 1922 – October 6, 2011) was an American [[physicist]], inventor, and a [[Professor Emeritus]] at [[Stevens Institute of Technology]]. His work on the [[many-body problem]] yielded a foundation of classical fluid [[statistical mechanics]], the [[Percus–Yevick approximation]]. He co-invented the first [[e-reader]] with Adnan Wally in 1972. He is also known for his contributions to [[David Bohm]]'s work in [[Quantum physics|quantum theory]].

Yevick was defeated in a run for the Democratic Party primary election for U.S. Congress in New Jersey in 1964.

== Early life and education ==
Yevick was born in [[Berwick, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=www.TownTopics.com — Obituaries |url=https://www.towntopics.com/backissues/oct1911/obits.php |access-date=2026-01-01 |website=www.towntopics.com}}</ref> He was of Jewish descent.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 27, 1961 |title=Federation of Organizations Sets Meeting Wednesday |work=The Jewish News |location=New Jersey |pages=21}}</ref> During the [[Great Depression in the United States|Great Depression]], George's [[Scout leader]] lent him money to attend the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1943 and a [[Doctor of Science]] in 1947 under the advisement of [[Victor Weisskopf]]<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/10992 |title=Biographical Memoirs |date=2004 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-08957-9 |volume=84 |location=Washington, D.C. |chapter=VICTOR FREDERICK WEISSKOPF |doi=10.17226/10992 |chapter-url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/10992/chapter/20}}</ref> at the [[MIT Radiation Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Yamin |first=David |date=April 8, 1988 |title=Teacher Feature |work=The Stute |pages=6 |publication-place=Hoboken, New Jersey}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> While at MIT, he met his wife [[Miriam Yevick]] ({{Nee|Lipschutz}}),<ref name=":0" /> a [[mathematician]] who had escaped from [[Antwerp]] in 1940 during the [[Nazi occupation of Belgium]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-11-09 |title=Guest lecturer, author recalls flight from fascism, shares life lessons |url=https://www.clarku.edu/news/2012/11/09/guest-lecturer-author-recalls-flight-from-fascism-shares-life-lessons/ |access-date=2025-12-03 |website=ClarkU News |language=en-US}}</ref> Their son, [[David Yevick|David]] and  granddaughter, [[Hannah Yevick|Hannah]], are also physicists.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yevick |first=David |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781118979792 |title=Fundamental Math and Physics for Scientists and Engineers |last2=Yevick |first2=Hannah |date= |publisher=Wiley |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-470-40784-4 |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.1002/9781118979792}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Yevick was appointed to the faculty at [[Stevens Institute of Technology]] in 1947.<ref>{{Cite news |date=June 25, 1947 |title=Stevens Makes Appointments |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1947/06/25/archives/stevens-makes-appointments.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> He spent his entire career there as a professor of Physics and Engineering Physics,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stevens Faculty Directory |url=https://web.stevens.edu/catalog/archive/2006_2007_Catalog/faculty_directory.html |access-date=2026-01-01 |website=web.stevens.edu}}</ref> and he became a [[Emeritus Professor]] in his retirement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Faculty (2003–2004) |url=https://web.stevens.edu/catalog/archive/2003_2004_Catalog/docs/Faculty_Directory.pdf |website=Stevens Institute of Technology}}</ref> They awarded him with an [[honorary degree]], a [[Master of Engineering]], in 1958.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Stevens Indicator, Winter 1995 |url=https://stevensarchives.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/StevensNP02/id/33756/ |access-date=2026-01-01 |website=stevensarchives.contentdm.oclc.org |language=en}}</ref>

In 1958, with [[Jerome K. Percus]], George co-authored a foundational study on classical fluid [[statistical mechanics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Percus |first=Jerome K. |last2=Yevick |first2=George J. |date=1958-04-01 |title=Analysis of Classical Statistical Mechanics by Means of Collective Coordinates |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.110.1 |journal=Physical Review |language=en |volume=110 |issue=1 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.110.1 |issn=0031-899X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This work was later named the [[Percus–Yevick approximation]] (PY). The approximation helped established a widely used family of liquid-state theories despite relying on uncontrolled approximations.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/publications/4886 |title=Mathematical Challenges from Theoretical/Computational Chemistry |date=1995-03-29 |publisher=National Academies Press |isbn=978-0-309-05097-5 |location=Washington, D.C. |chapter=Mathematical Research Opportunities from Theoretical/Computational Chemistry |doi=10.17226/4886}}</ref> With the [[hypernetted-chain equation]], the PY is a foundational closure approximation for computing [[radial distribution function]]s and related thermodynamic properties of dense fluids.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Battimelli |first=Giovanni |title=Computer meets theoretical physics: the new frontier of molecular simulation |last2=Ciccotti |first2=Giovanni |last3=Greco |first3=Pietro |date=2020 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-030-39399-1 |series=The frontiers collection |location=Cham}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=|page=70}}

Yevick and his wife corresponded frequently with [[David Bohm]] while he was at [[University of São Paulo]]. They are most known for contributing to and circulating Bohm's [[De Broglie–Bohm theory|causal interpretation of quantum theory]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Peat |first=F. David |title=Infinite potential: the life and times of David Bohm |date=1997 |publisher=Addison Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-40635-1 |series=Helix books |location=Reading, Mass}}</ref> Bohm also asked for Yevick's thoughts on his theory of [[luminiferous aether]] as a unification of physics using [[Plasma (physics)|plasma physics]] in relation to [[general relativity]], [[quantum field theory]] and [[vacuum energy]]. From Yevick's wife, Bohm requested a [[mathematical proof]] to support a statistical mechanics argument that rare exceptions are negligible, such that typical behavior could be treated as physically reliable.<ref>{{Citation |last=Talbot |first=Chris |chapter=Single Pages of Letters to Miriam Yevick and Letter to George Yevick |date=2017 |title=David Bohm: Causality and Chance, Letters to Three Women |pages=437–446 |editor-last=Talbot |editor-first=Chris |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-55492-1_33 |access-date=2026-01-01 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-55492-1_33 |isbn=978-3-319-55491-4|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Yevick's work was later used in [[Holographic principle|holographic]] theories of [[spacetime]] developed by [[David Finkelstein]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Finkelstein |first=David |date=1972-06-15 |title=Space-Time Code. III |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevD.5.2922 |journal=Physical Review D |language=en |volume=5 |issue=12 |pages=2922–2931 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.5.2922 |issn=0556-2821|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Inventions ===
Yevick developed more than 40 [[patent]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Patents by Inventor George J. Yevick |url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/george-j-yevick |website=Justia}}</ref> In 1972, Yevick, with Adnan Wally, co-invented the first [[e-reader]], which had an [[LCD]] that was resistant to washout. It was publicized on the front page of ''[[The New York Times]]'' and predicted to revolutionize the publishing industry.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Greene |first=Nick |date=2015-01-08 |title=The Forgotten Early E-Book |url=https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/61005/revolutionary-e-book-never-got-chance-be-read |access-date=2026-01-01 |website=Mental Floss |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sullivan |first=Walter |date=November 25, 1972 |title=New Microfilm Method Puts Book on a Sheet of Film |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1972/11/25/archives/new-jersey-pages-new-microfilm-method-puts-book-on-a-sheet-of-film.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> However, the invention happened in parallel with the onset of the development of [[ebook]]s by [[Michael S. Hart]]<ref>{{Cite news |last=Flood |first=Alison |date=2011-09-08 |title=Michael Hart, inventor of the ebook, dies aged 64 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2011/sep/08/michael-hart-inventor-ebook-dies |access-date=2026-01-01 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> and personal computing devices, overshadowing the work and preventing its commercialization.<ref name=":2" />

== Politics and advocacy ==
Yevick advocated for establishing a science and technology museum in New York City based on an educational model, featuring interactive exhibits and modern audiovisual interpretation to demonstrate basic scientific principles to the public.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Thomas |first=W. Stephen |date=August 24, 1959 |title=Need for Science Museums; Move to Erect Technical Center in New York Suggested |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1959/08/24/archives/need-for-science-museums-move-to-erect-technical-center-in-new-york.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

A resident of [[Leonia, New Jersey]], Yevick ran as a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] in the [[primary election|primary]] of the [[1964 United States House of Representatives elections]] for a seat for [[New Jersey's 9th congressional district]].<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-news-area-news-highlights/188116858/ "Area News Highlights"], ''[[Herald News]]'', March 6, 1964. Accessed January 3, 2026, via [[Newspapers.com]]. "Dr. George Yevick of Leonia is running for the 9th Congressional District post held by Rep. Frank Osmers, possibly in opposition to Independent-Democrat Mayor Henry Helstoski of East Rutherford, the Democrats' candidate."</ref> He was defeated by [[Henry Helstoski]].<ref>{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=April 22, 1964 |title=Negro Nominated In Jersey Voting; Stubbs, Newark Republican, to Run for House Seat |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/04/22/archives/negro-nominated-in-jersey-voting-stubbs-newark-republican-to-run.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> His platform was centered around [[civil rights]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 27, 1964 |title=Fair Housing Unit to Hear Speaker |work=The Record |pages=27 |publication-place=Hackensack, New Jersey}}</ref> He was the elected chair of the New Jersey Democratic Council,<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 15, 1967 |title=Group Schedules Viet Program |work=The Jewish News |location=New Jersey |pages=35}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Sullivan |first=Ronald |date=December 3, 1967 |title=War Foes Begin Drive In Jersey; Seek Democrats to Oppose Johnson in Primary Plans 4 Primary Races |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1967/12/03/archives/war-foes-begin-drive-in-jersey-seek-democrats-to-oppose-johnson-in.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> an [[Anti-war movement|anti-war]] political group of [[Reform Democrat]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wu |first=Judy Tzu-Chun |title=Radicals on the road: internationalism, orientalism, and feminism during the Vietnam Era |date=2013 |publisher=Cornell University Press |isbn=978-0-8014-4675-7 |location=Ithaca |chapter=Searching for Home and Peace}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=|page=99|location=}}
